title: Is It a Fair Test?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Science · Claims, variables and bias
objective: Students will use the story the exhibition tells in *QWERTY’s Accidental Empire* to learn what makes a test fair. August Dvorak claimed his keyboard could raise typing speed by 74%; a Navy test overseen by Dvorak himself reported dramatic improvements; a 1956 government study found no real advantage. Students will name the **variables**, the **controls** and the **bias** in tests like these, find a problem in the Typing Station’s own race, and design a fair test of their own.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every day you hear claims that something is faster, better or proven. Knowing what makes a test fair lets you decide for yourself.

items.text: explain why a claim, like Dvorak’s 74%, needs a fair test before we believe it
items.question: explain why Dvorak’s claim needed a fair test?

items.text: identify bias and a variable that could spoil a test, such as who runs it or the order of turns
items.question: spot bias, or a variable that could spoil a test?

items.text: design a fair test that changes one variable, keeps the others the same, and measures a result
items.question: design a fair test with one variable changed and the rest kept the same?

items.text: evaluate a claim that says only *studies suggest*, and say what evidence would settle it
items.question: say what evidence would settle a claim that only says studies suggest?

materials: The *Claims and tests* page on page 3, projected or printed
The Typing Station on the exhibition website, and a clock or timer
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** at the Typing Station, race the machines, then race again. Did your second time improve? Post your class’s times to the class board, and ask: is that enough evidence to call one machine faster?

steps.title: 74% faster?
script: Read Dvorak’s claim from the poster: *“Challengers emerged: August Dvorak created a scientifically "superior" keyboard in 1936 that placed the most common letters on the home row, claiming it could increase typing speed by 74%.”* Ask: *“Would you switch keyboards? What would you need to know first?”* Collect what students would want to know: who tested it, on whom, how. Keep the list for the debrief.

screen.text: Challengers emerged: August Dvorak created a scientifically "superior" keyboard in 1936 that placed the most common letters on the home row, claiming it could increase typing speed by 74%.

steps.purpose: Start with a striking claim and the instinct to believe it.
students: Would you switch keyboards? What would you need to know first?

steps.title: Two tests
script: Read: *“The U.S. Navy tested it during World War II and reported dramatic improvements, though the study was overseen by Dvorak himself and a 1956 government study found no real advantage.”* Show the *Claims and tests* table. Ask: *who oversaw the Navy test?* Name **bias**: when the person running a test wants a certain answer, the result can lean toward it, even without anyone meaning to cheat. Name **replication**: an independent test of the same claim.

Define the parts of a fair test: the **independent variable** (the one thing you change, here the keyboard), the **dependent variable** (what you measure, here typing speed) and the **controlled variables** (everything you keep the same: the text, the typists, the time).

screen.caption: One claim, two tests, as QWERTY’s Accidental Empire tells it

cells: August Dvorak’s keyboard could increase typing speed by 74%.

steps.purpose: Compare two tests of one claim, and notice who ran each.

steps.title: Is the race fair?
script: Open the Typing Station’s race. It says: *“Type the line on the typewriter first: the clock starts at your first key.”* then the iMac. Ask: *if you type the same line twice, will the second try be easier?* That is an **order effect**: practice could make the second machine look faster. Ask how to fix it.

screen.alt: The Typing Station room: a typewriter on the coral wall, its first line typed on the sheet of paper, with the tabs Typewriter, iMac, Top row and Class Board
screen.caption: The Typing Station: a race on the typewriter, then on the iMac

steps.purpose: Find a flaw in a test students can run themselves: the order of the turns.
students: The typewriter always goes first. Does that help or hurt the iMac?
How could you make the race fair?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three judge the same tests; each ends with a test students could run.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Answer who claimed and who tested, match three science words to their meanings, and plan a fair handwriting-or-typing race with a guided frame.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare the two studies, fix the order effect in the Typing Station race, and design a fair test of the poster’s claim about printed pages and memory.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Find the confounding variable of muscle memory, count the letters on each keyboard row as data, and question a claim that only says *studies suggest*.

steps.purpose: Judge the tests in the exhibition, then design a fair one.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three end with a test you could run.

steps.title: Convince me
script: Return to the hook’s list. Ask: *“What would it take to convince you that one keyboard is faster than another?”* Expect: tested by someone with no stake in the result, typists who start equal, the same text, many people, the order of turns mixed.

screen.question: What would it take to convince you that one keyboard is faster than another?

steps.purpose: Return to the hook’s list, now in the language of fair tests.
students: Name the variable you would change.
Name two things you would keep the same.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
